topic.angle: The 1202 alarm and a computer that dropped low-priority work

card.title: The alarm that didn't stop the landing

panels.text: 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin are descending toward the Moon in the lunar module Eagle, guided by the Apollo Guidance Computer.
Minutes before landing, the computer flashes alarms numbered 1202 and 1201. They are unexpected.
In Houston, guidance officer Steve Bales, advised by Jack Garman, has to decide quickly: abort or continue?
The twist: the computer was overloaded, but it had been designed to drop lower-priority tasks and keep the critical ones running. Bales said go, and Eagle landed.

probes.question: What did the Apollo computer do when it became overloaded?
options: Dropped low-priority tasks and kept critical ones running

probes.question: True or false: the 1202 alarm forced Apollo 11 to abort the landing.

image_brief.show: The Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle on the Moon or in descent, or the Apollo Guidance Computer's DSKY panel

claims.claim: 20 July 1969: Armstrong and Aldrin descending in lunar module Eagle guided by the AGC
claims.quote: Eagle landed and Armstrong shut the engine down.

claims.claim: Computer flashed 1202 and 1201 alarms minutes before landing
claims.quote: the LM guidance computer (LGC) distracted the crew with the first of several unexpected 1201 and 1202 program alarms.
claims.note: About five minutes into the descent burn.

claims.claim: Nobody in the crew had seen them in a real descent
claims.note: Neither fetched text says this. Suggest dropping, or: 'The alarms were unexpected.'

claims.claim: Steve Bales was a 'young' guidance officer with 'seconds' to decide
claims.note: Sources name Bales as Guidance Officer/controller but say nothing of age or seconds; Apollo 11 page says Jack Garman judged it safe and told Bales. Suggest: 'Guidance officer Steve Bales, advised by Jack Garman, had to decide quickly.'

claims.claim: Computer was overloaded but designed to drop lower-priority tasks and keep critical ones
claims.quote: The AGC software had been designed with priority scheduling, and automatically recovered, deleting lower priority tasks.

claims.claim: Bales said go and Eagle landed
claims.quote: issued several 'GO' calls and the landing was successful.

claims.claim: Probe 1: computer dropped low-priority tasks and kept critical ones running
claims.note: Distractor 'Shut down and restarted' is partly true (software restart per source); consider rewording distractor.

claims.claim: Probe 2: 1202 alarm did not force an abort
claims.quote: issued several 'GO' calls and the landing was successful.
